reason: The provided sources give well over 10 cross-verified claims across independent sites detailing the discovery, mechanism, velocity, gamma-ray eclipses, and revised mass of the original Black Widow pulsar PSR B1957+20.
story: In 1988, astronomers discovered PSR B1957+20, a rapidly spinning neutron star known as a millisecond pulsar. Orbiting a low-mass companion star every 9.2 hours, the pulsar completes a full rotation in just 1.6 milliseconds. As it speeds through space at nearly one million kilometers per hour, it generates a supersonic bow shock visible to optical telescopes. But the dead star is doing something even more sinister: it blasts its companion with an intense wind of radiation and high-energy particles, slowly evaporating the companion's outer layers into space. Because it destroys the companion star that originally helped spin it up, scientists nicknamed it the Black Widow pulsar. Initial optical modeling suggested the pulsar had an ultra-heavy mass of 2.4 solar masses, but NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope later detected a gamma-ray eclipse, establishing its true mass at roughly 1.8 solar masses.
angle: A dead star spinning over 600 times per second blasts its companion star with a relativistic particle beam, slowly vaporizing it down to nothing.

claims.claim: The original Black Widow pulsar (PSR B1957+20) was discovered in 1988.
Pulsars are rapidly spinning neutron stars created from collapsed stellar cores.
Black widow pulsars destroy or evaporate their companion stars through intense particle winds and radiation.
The companion star of PSR B1957+20 orbits the pulsar with a period of 9.2 hours.
PSR B1957+20 has a rapid rotation period of approximately 1.6 milliseconds.
The 'black widow' moniker comes from the spider species known for killing its mate.
Companion stars in black widow systems have very low masses, often brown dwarfs or under 0.1 solar masses.
Redback pulsars form a related class of spider pulsars with companion stars more massive than those of black widows.
Neutron stars are spun up into rapid millisecond pulsars by pulling material off their companions.
PSR B1957+20 travels through space at a speed of nearly one million kilometers per hour.
Optical telescopes detect an H-alpha bow shock ahead of PSR B1957+20 as it moves through interstellar gas.
X-ray observatories like Chandra detected an elongated cloud or shock structure behind PSR B1957+20.
The Fermi Large Area Telescope observed gamma-ray eclipses from spider pulsars, including PSR B1957+20.
Gamma-ray eclipse data revised PSR B1957+20's mass down from an estimated 2.4 solar masses to about 1.8 solar masses.
Astronomers have discovered dozens of black widow pulsar systems across the galaxy.

disputed: Mass of PSR B1957+20: Early optical light curve modeling estimated its mass at roughly 2.4 solar masses, whereas direct gamma-ray eclipse measurements constrained it to 1.81 solar masses. Script should handle this as: 'Early estimates suggested it was an ultra-massive 2.4 solar masses, but gamma-ray observations updated its true mass to about 1.8 solar masses.'
